newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Analysts sceptical of POSCO offer on Hanbo Steel.
newsitem.headline: Analysts sceptical of POSCO offer on Hanbo Steel.

text.p: Speculation continued on Tuesday about the future of South Korea's Hanbo Steel Co despite Pohang Iron and Steel Co's (POSCO) offer to buy the failed company's assets, analysts said.
After the second auction to sell off Hanbo failed with no bids received by the 0600 GMT deadline on Tuesday, POSCO's proposal remains the only offer on the table.
But analysts doubted that Hanbo's creditor banks would accept the offer after a POSCO executive estimated the failed steelmaker's value at about half of what an accounting firm had said it was worth.
"Creditor banks are unlikely to accept the offer," said Choi Hyoung-won, a financial analyst at LG Securities. "Instead, they will become more aggressive to secure a takeover."
A third-party takeover would keep Hanbo's bank loans classified as redeemable, while a sale of assets only would create a huge loan loss for creditor banks, analysts said.

After no bidders showed up for Tuesday's auction, POSCO executive manager Park Chong-il told a news conference POSCO had estimated the price for the purchase of Hanbo's fixed assets at about two trillion won ($2.24 billion).
This compares to an accounting firm's evaluation of 4.15 trillion won for Hanbo's fixed assets.
An official with Hanbo's main creditor, Korea First Bank, said Park's estimate was disappointing.

"It's too early to talk about the price but the estimate is disappointing when compared with the accounting firm's evaluation," Lee Keun-hee, who heads Korea First's taskforce to sell Hanbo, told the news conference.

Analysts said creditor banks were now expected to offer more favourable conditions for a takeover because they might view POSCO's offer as government pressure. The government is the largest single shareholder of POSCO.
But creditor banks are facing increasing international pressure to reduce their non-performing loans.

Cyprus-based Capital Intelligence said on Tuesday it had downgraded Korea First Bank's long-term rating to BB plus from BBB minus. Two other credit-rating agencies have said they are reviewing several big Korean banks for possible downgrading.
Analysts said POSCO's offer did not eliminate the possibility that the Hyundai Group might make a bid.

"From the beginning, the auctions have been viewed as the procedural way to complete a sale that was agreed to through private negotiations," said an analyst at a local securities firm who declined to be identified.
"I think Hanbo will in the end be sold through private negotiations," said Peter Lee, an analyst at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
Hyundai, the nation's largest conglomerate, has said it was not interested in taking over Hanbo, but that is still viewed as an ideal solution.
Analysts said Hyundai, which wants to build an integrated steel mill, needed to enhance its image as a contributor to the national economy by sharing the country's troubles.
They said the possibility remained for Hyundai either to join the consortium that POSCO would form or to take over Hanbo on its own at the last minute at a reduced price.
"What worries POSCO is a situation in which it has to solely take over Hanbo while Hyundai is seen to be waiting for better conditions," said Lee of Dongbang.

The government has not directly opposed Hyundai's moves to enter the steel industry in public, but it has said it is concerned about oversupply of steel and the concentration of economic power in big conglomerates.
POSCO has been running Hanbo Steel on behalf of creditors since April, three months after it was declared insolvent with debts of some five trillion won.
(Conversion: $1 = 891.90 won)
